posts.title: Splitting the birch for winter
posts.excerpt: Two tonnes of wood, three Sunday mornings and one very old axe.
posts.content:
The birch comes down from the hills in October, still wet. We stack it in the lane behind the bathhouse and split it on Sunday mornings before the stove is lit.

Split wood dries twice as fast. By January it burns clean and hot, and the room smells faintly sweet, which is how the regulars know it is the new season’s wood.

posts.title: Why the plunge is sixteen degrees
posts.excerpt: We never chill the water. The well decides, and it has been right for sixty years.
posts.content:
People ask why our plunge is not colder. Some saunas keep theirs at ten degrees; ours comes straight from the bathhouse well and stays near sixteen all year.

At sixteen you can stay a full minute without gasping, and that minute is what makes the rest on the roof so deep. Colder is not better; slower is.

posts.title: Hinoki shavings for the autumn löyly
posts.excerpt: A carpenter down the lane saves us a bag of shavings every week.
posts.content:
From September the löyly bucket smells of hinoki. The shavings come from a carpenter four doors down, who planes cypress for bath tubs and gives us what falls on his floor.

We steep a handful overnight in well water. On the stones it turns into a soft, clean steam that lingers on the roof for a minute after you go up.
